subtitle: The Passive · Processes · Graphs · Cause and Effect · Noun Formation

blocks.narration: Welcome to the complete video guide for English for Engineering One, weeks five to seven. In the next half hour you will master four big tools of technical English: the passive voice for describing processes, the language of graphs and charts, cause and effect with its prepositions, and word formation for comparing solutions, plus the signposting phrases that hold a short talk together. Every rule comes from your course files, every example is real lecture material, and it is all aimed straight at Test Two. Let's begin.

blocks.title: The Passive — Form and Use
blocks.subtitle: Who did it? Often we don't say.
blocks.narration: Chapter one. The passive voice. Why do engineers say 'a hole is made using a drill' and never mention who made it? Because in a process, the steps matter more than the person. This chapter builds the whole passive system: its form, its uses, the agent 'by', and all the tenses you need.

blocks.heading: What Is the Passive?
bullets: Form: be + past participle
The object becomes the new subject
Use it when the doer is unknown
A lot of films are shot on location.
blocks.narration: So what exactly is the passive? The form never changes: the verb 'be' plus a past participle. 'A lot of films are shot on location.' In a passive sentence, the object of the active verb moves to the front and becomes the new subject. We use the passive when it isn't said, known, or important who does the action. Somebody stole Artem's bike, but we don't know who, so English says 'Artem's bike has been stolen.' And negatives and questions are formed exactly as in active sentences: 'Some films aren't shot on location.' 'Is your car being repaired today?'

blocks.heading: Active or Passive — Two Ways of Focusing
rows: Aztec boys were trained to fight.
The police are questioning two men.
blocks.narration: Active or passive — they are two ways of focusing on the same event. 'Ridley Scott directed Napoleon' puts the director in the spotlight. 'Napoleon was directed by Ridley Scott' puts the film first — that is the sentence you use when the film is your topic. The same shift happens with 'Teachers trained Aztec boys' and its passive version 'Aztec boys were trained to fight,' where the boys, not the teachers, are the point. And in 'The police are questioning two men,' the real news is the men, so the passive says 'Two men are being questioned.' Choose the voice that puts your topic in first position.

blocks.heading: Four Reasons to Choose the Passive
bullets: Move important information to the front
Be impersonal — don't name the doer
The doer is obvious (teachers, people)
Formal and technical style prefers it
blocks.narration: The worksheet gives four situations where the passive is the right choice. First, to move the important information — the object of the active sentence — to the beginning: 'Two men are being questioned by the police.' Second, to be impersonal, when you do not want to name the person who performs the action. Third, when the doer is obvious, like teachers, or too general, like 'people' or 'they': 'Aztec boys were trained to fight.' And fourth, the passive is more common in formal speech and writing — science and engineering use it constantly.

blocks.heading: The Agent 'by' and the Instrument 'with'
bullets: by + person: only when the agent matters
The hall will be opened by the King.
with + object that performs the action
The game was played with a rubber ball.
blocks.narration: If we do want to say who did the action, we add the agent with 'by' — but only when it is really necessary. 'The new concert hall will be opened by the King' — the King matters here. 'The two men were arrested' — the police are obvious, so no 'by.' For instruments, objects that perform the action, use 'with': 'The game was played with a ball of solid rubber.' Real agents are worth naming: 'Some countries have been harmed by tourism'; 'many buildings in the city have been damaged by the earthquake.'

blocks.heading: The Passive in Five Tenses
rows: Oil and gas are found underground.
When is our car being repaired?
The film will be shot in autumn.
blocks.narration: The passive works in every tense you need. Present simple, for processes that are generally true: 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea.' Present continuous, for actions happening now: 'When is our car being repaired?' Past simple, for finished events: 'The first English dictionary was written in sixteen-oh-four.' Present perfect, connecting past to now: 'Some countries have been harmed by tourism.' And 'will,' for the future: 'The film will be shot in the autumn.' The rule is always the same: keep the tense of 'be,' add the past participle.

blocks.heading: Transform: Active to Passive
blocks.problem: They subtitle a lot of foreign films.

steps.text: Active: They subtitle a lot of foreign films.
Find the object: a lot of foreign films
Passive: A lot of foreign films are subtitled.

blocks.result: A lot of foreign films are subtitled.
blocks.narration: Let's transform an active sentence step by step. 'They subtitle a lot of foreign films.' Step one: find the object of the verb — 'a lot of foreign films.' Step two: move it to the front; it becomes the new subject. Step three: put the verb into the passive — the new subject is plural, so 'are,' plus the past participle 'subtitled.' The general subject 'they' disappears, because it is unnecessary. The result: 'A lot of foreign films are subtitled.' And remember: this only works with transitive verbs, verbs that have an object. 'I lost my wallet' can become passive; 'I swim every day' cannot — there is nothing to move.

blocks.heading: Active or Passive — Circle the Correct Form
blocks.problem: Circle the correct form, active or passive (items from the lecture).

steps.text: The costumes are being made by hand.
His latest film is set in Vietnam.
The photo was taken by my husband.
Ask: does the subject perform or undergo?

blocks.narration: Now the reverse skill: choosing the correct form. 'The costumes for the show are making, or are being made, by hand' — the costumes undergo the action, so 'are being made.' 'The story inspired, or was inspired, him' — the story performs the action, so active: 'inspired.' 'His latest film is set in Vietnam' — passive. 'The actors aren't recording the dialogue' — the actors perform the action, so active. 'The photo was taken by my husband' — passive, with an agent. The rule of thumb: if the subject undergoes the action and the doer is unknown or unimportant, choose the passive; if the subject performs the action, keep the active.

items: The object becomes the new subject
Only transitive verbs can be passive
blocks.narration: Chapter one in four lines. The passive is 'be' plus past participle. The object of the active sentence becomes the new subject. Use 'by' for the agent when it matters, and 'with' for the instrument. And only transitive verbs — verbs with an object — can be made passive. That is the whole engine; next we put it to work.

blocks.title: Describing Processes and Sequences
blocks.subtitle: How engineering says how things are made
blocks.narration: Chapter two. Describing processes and sequences. How is a check valve manufactured? How is tea made? Engineers describe processes with the present simple passive and a small set of sequencing words. This chapter gives you the manufacturing vocabulary and two model texts: a solar radiation text and a tea factory.

blocks.heading: Manufacturing Processes
rows: A hole is made using a drill.
Hot liquid is poured and cooled.
Pieces are joined at high heat.
Material is turned on a lathe.
Parts joined with nut and bolt.
blocks.narration: Here is the lecture's manufacturing vocabulary, and notice the grammar: every description is a passive sentence in the present simple. Drilling: a hole is made using a drill. Casting: hot liquid material is poured into a container and cooled to make the correct shape. Welding: two pieces are joined together using very high temperature. Turning: the material is turned on a machine called a lathe, and part of it is removed. Pressing: a material is pressed into the correct shape. Bolting: two pieces are joined with a nut and a bolt. The lecture adds punching, painting, polishing and inspection — the same pattern every time.

blocks.heading: Why the Passive Fits Processes
bullets: The steps matter, not the person
Who does it: not said, known, important
The standard form in technical writing
Oil and gas are found beneath the sea.
blocks.narration: Why does engineering love the passive? Because in a technical process, the steps matter more than the person doing them. Who drills the hole is not said, not known, and not important — so the doer disappears from the sentence. That is why the passive is the standard way to describe scientific and technical processes: 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea.' 'A hole is made using a drill.' The listener follows the sequence of operations, and nothing distracts from it. This is why technical instructions and lab reports prefer the passive voice.

blocks.heading: A Check Valve Is Made
blocks.problem: Describe the manufacturing process of a check valve.

steps.text: First, the body of the valve is cast.
Then it is turned on a lathe.
After that, the parts are bolted together.

blocks.narration: Here is the full model answer for the check valve, exactly the style the lecture expects. First, the body of the valve is cast from hot metal and cooled to make the correct shape. Then it is turned on a lathe, and part of the material is removed. Next, a hole is drilled, and the parts are bolted together with a nut and a bolt. After that, the valve is painted. Finally, the work is checked carefully — the valve is inspected. Three things carry this description: the present simple passive, the sequencing words, and the passive focus on the valve itself, never on a worker. Copy this pattern for any process you are asked to describe.

blocks.heading: Sequencing a Process
bullets: Adverbs: firstly, then, next, finally
after that — the middle of a sequence
as soon as / once / when link events
At this stage, the water boils.
blocks.narration: A process needs a clear order, and English gives you three tools. Sequencing adverbs: 'firstly,' 'then,' 'next,' 'after that,' 'finally' — 'Firstly, some energy is removed by the clouds.' Conjunctions that show how two events relate to each other: 'after,' 'as,' 'as soon as,' 'once,' 'when' — 'As soon as sunlight hits the flower, its petals open.' And the phrase 'at this stage' to mark a clear point in the process: 'The temperature reaches one hundred degrees. At this stage, the water in the container begins to boil.' Say them aloud until they come automatically.

blocks.heading: Solar Radiation — a Model Text
bullets: 25% is reflected by clouds and atmosphere
A further 20% is absorbed by them
5% is reflected from the Earth's surface
Finally, 50% is absorbed by the surface
blocks.narration: The week's model text describes solar radiation, and it is a masterclass in process language. As solar radiation travels to Earth, a series of steps reduce it. Firstly, around twenty-five percent is reflected by the upper atmosphere and clouds. Then, a further twenty percent is absorbed by them. At this stage, five percent is reflected back from the Earth's surface, by deserts or ice. Finally, fifty percent is absorbed by the Earth's surface itself. Ten percent of this heat radiates from the surface, the remaining forty percent moves to the clouds, and the heat is radiated back into space, completing the cycle. Learn the three key verbs: absorb, to take in energy; emit, to send it out; reflect, to send it back.

blocks.heading: How Is Tea Made?
blocks.problem: Put the stages of tea production in order (orthodox method).

steps.text: They are taken to a nearby factory.
They are withered — moisture is lost.
Finally, they are dried, graded, packed.

blocks.narration: Now the reading text: how is tea made? First, the leaves are plucked — picked from the plant — and taken quickly to a factory near the tea garden, because they must be processed before they lose their moisture. In the factory, the leaves are withered: they lose water and become soft and weak. Then they are rolled, and oxidized: the enzymes inside the leaves react with the air, the colour changes from green to brown, and the flavour develops. This stage decides how dark and strong the tea will be. Finally, the leaves are dried, graded and packed into tea chests. Green tea skips oxidation — the leaves are heated so the enzymes stop working. And CTC tea? Crushed, torn and curled into small granules.

items: firstly, then, next, after that, finally
as soon as / once / when — two events
at this stage marks a clear point
blocks.narration: Chapter two in short. Manufacturing and natural processes are described with the present simple passive. Order the steps with 'firstly,' 'then,' 'next,' 'after that,' 'finally.' Link two events with 'as soon as,' 'once,' or 'when.' And mark a key moment with 'at this stage.' With these tools, any process you meet can be described clearly and in the right order.

blocks.title: Understanding Graphs and Charts
blocks.subtitle: The vocabulary engineers use for data
blocks.narration: Chapter three. Understanding graphs and charts. Data speaks through diagrams, and engineers must name them, read their axes, and describe movement precisely. This chapter covers diagram types, the movement verbs and nouns, the adjective and adverb pairs, and the little preposition rule that so many students lose marks on.

blocks.heading: Diagrams and Figures
bullets: Diagrams present data concisely
In articles: Fig. 1, Fig. 2 (figures)
Pie chart — a circle of segments
Bar chart — bars of equal width
blocks.narration: Diagrams are visual ways of presenting data concisely; in academic articles they are usually labelled 'Figure one,' 'Figure two.' A pie chart is a circle divided into segments from the middle, like slices of a cake, with a key or legend showing what each segment represents. A bar chart uses thin vertical or horizontal bars of the same width, whose height or length varies with the amounts. A histogram is a bar chart where the bar width also varies. A table is a grid of columns and rows, a cross-section shows the inside of something cut across the middle, and a flowchart indicates the stages of a process.

blocks.heading: Which Diagram Do You Need?
blocks.narration: Which diagram fits which task? If you show the parts of a total, use a pie chart. If you compare amounts, use a bar chart. For the stages of a process, a flowchart. To show layers inside something, like the rock layers of the Grand Canyon, a cross-section — with a label for each part. For numbers in a grid, a table, where columns run vertically and rows run horizontally. One warning from the lecture: no definite article with a numbered figure — 'See Figure three,' never 'See the Figure three.'

blocks.heading: Axes, Points and Lines
bullets: Vertical (y) axis; horizontal (x) axis
Points are plotted, then joined
Two lines cross — they intersect
Parallel lines never intersect
blocks.narration: Graphs are drawn by plotting points and then drawing a line to join adjacent points. Line and bar charts have a vertical axis and a horizontal axis, and each axis is labelled to show what it contains: age, weight, height, date, time, length, percentage, duration. If two lines cross, they intersect at a point; lines that run parallel to one another never intersect. And 'adjacent' means directly next to each other — adjacent points, adjacent columns. If you survey people, you take a sample; the pocket-money study used a random sample of one thousand teenagers.

blocks.heading: Movement — Verbs and Nouns
blocks.narration: Every movement has a verb and a noun. Going up: 'sales have risen' — 'we've experienced a rise'; 'sales have climbed over the past two quarters'; 'consumer confidence recovered' — 'a recovery'; 'there has been an increase of twenty-three percent since June.' Going down: 'research spending has fallen by thirty percent' — 'a fall'; 'we've seen a decline over the past three months'; 'sales have plunged in the northwest region' — 'a plunge'; 'government spending has decreased by ten percent.' For the future, use 'project,' 'forecast,' 'predict': 'we project improved sales,' 'we forecast increased spending,' 'we predict improving sales through June.'

blocks.heading: Big Movers and Their Opposites
bullets: soar — rise fast; plummet (opposite)
double — twice; halve (opposite)
exceed — go above; fall below
appreciate — rise in value; depreciate
blocks.narration: Now the strong verbs, each with its opposite. 'Soar' means to increase very quickly and by a large amount; its opposite is 'plummet' — populations of some bird species have plummeted by ninety-seven percent. 'Double' means to increase to twice the number; its opposite is 'halve' — the value of a family car has more than halved after three years. 'Exceed' means to increase to greater than a particular number — the temperature exceeded forty-five degrees; its opposite is 'fall below.' And 'appreciate' means to increase in value, like land on the edge of the city; its opposite is 'depreciate' — that car depreciates by twenty percent per year.

blocks.heading: increase by / increase of / increase in
bullets: Verb: The population increased by 10%.
Noun + of: an increase of 15%
Noun + in: an increase in car use
An increase of 12% in smart phone sales
blocks.narration: Here is the preposition rule that appears in the test. With a verb, 'increase' and 'decrease' take 'by' for the size of the change: 'the population of the city has increased by ten percent.' With a noun, use 'of' for the size and 'in' for what is rising: 'a rise of fifteen percent in the number of cars.' So the correct sentence is 'an increase of twelve percent in smart phone sales' — 'of' for the size, 'in' for the thing that is changing. The version with 'in' before the percentage is the trap answer in the lecture's question.

blocks.heading: Adjectives and Adverbs of Change
blocks.narration: Adjectives describe the shape of a change; adverbs describe how it happens; pair them and your description becomes precise. 'There has been a slight decline in sales' — 'sales have declined slightly.' 'Investment rose sharply during the first quarter' — 'a sharp increase in investment.' 'Sales dropped abruptly in March' — 'an abrupt drop.' 'Consumer interest suddenly decreased' — 'a sudden decrease in consumer interest.' 'We dramatically improved customer satisfaction' — 'the dramatic growth came after we invested in a new product line.' And steady: 'a steady improvement' — 'sales have improved steadily since March.' When nothing changes at all, profit is flat.

blocks.heading: Describe the West City Chart
blocks.problem: The chart shows cars entering downtown West City each day, years 1–8.

steps.text: The chart shows the number of cars…
Car numbers rose for the first years
Explained by a new railway in year 6

blocks.narration: Time to describe a real chart, following the lecture's pocket-money model: first what the graph presents, then the axes, then the trend, then the explanation. 'The chart shows the number of cars entering the downtown area of West City each day over an eight-year period. The totals are listed on the vertical, or y, axis, while the years are listed on the horizontal, or x, axis. From the graph we see the general trend: car use rose and then fell over the period. The number of cars rose for the first few years and then declined after year six. The decline can be explained by the fact that a new mass transit railway was opened in year six.' Present, axes, trend, explanation — that is the four-move pattern.

blocks.heading: Rewrite with Movement Verbs
blocks.problem: Rewrite using precise movement verbs (and find the mistake).

steps.text: The mistake: See the figure 3 → Figure 3

blocks.narration: Now rewrite plain phrases with precise verbs. 'Populations have crashed by ninety-seven percent' becomes 'have plummeted by ninety-seven percent,' and 'the number of cases has increased sharply' becomes 'has soared.' 'The child mortality rate fell to lower than sixty deaths per thousand' becomes 'fell below sixty.' 'House prices have gone up rapidly by a large amount' becomes 'have soared.' 'The temperature rose higher than forty-five degrees' becomes 'exceeded forty-five degrees.' And the deliberate mistake: 'See the figure three' must lose its 'the' — it is 'See Figure three.' One more from this activity: 'business courses have multiplied while science programmes have declined.' That article error is exactly what the test loves to catch.

items: increase BY 10%; increase OF 15% IN sales
blocks.narration: Chapter three in five lines. Name your diagram: pie chart, bar chart, table, flowchart, cross-section. Plot the points, join them, and know whether lines intersect or run parallel. Use the strong pairs: soar and plummet, double and halve, exceed and fall below. Remember: increased by ten percent, but an increase of fifteen percent in sales. And never write 'the Figure three.'

blocks.title: Cause and Effect
blocks.subtitle: Verbs and nouns that link reason and result
blocks.narration: Chapter four. Cause and effect. Why did sales fall? What triggered the explosion? Engineers explain results every day, and English has a rich family of cause-and-effect verbs and nouns — each with its own preposition. Master them, and your explanations sound professional.

blocks.heading: Cause-and-Effect Verbs
bullets: influence: Her grandmother influenced Sarah
determine — the main factor deciding it
motivate — makes them want to do it
facilitate — makes it easier
blocks.narration: The first family of cause verbs. 'Influence' takes a direct object, with no preposition: 'Her grandmother influenced Sarah's choice of career' — and as a noun it takes 'on.' 'Determine' means to be the main factor: 'parental attitude largely determines how well a child adapts to school.' 'Motivate' means to make someone want to do something positive: 'a good teacher motivates their students.' 'Facilitate' means to make easier: 'the flow of traffic through the town is facilitated by the one-way system.' And 'generate' means to cause something to happen or exist: 'her exhibition generated a lot of interest.'

blocks.heading: More Cause Verbs
bullets: provoke — cause, usually negative
trigger — start, sudden, negative
inhibit — hold back, prevent
induce — cause, often medical
blocks.narration: The second family. 'Provoke' means to cause, usually something negative: 'his speech provoked an angry response.' 'Trigger' means to start, usually something sudden and negative: 'the explosion was triggered by the heat.' 'Inhibit' means to prevent, to hold back: 'a teacher's presence can often inhibit teenagers' discussions.' 'Induce' means to cause, often in a medical context: 'the drugs may induce nausea.' And 'stimulate' means to cause something to develop or function: 'their child was given drugs to stimulate growth.' Together with 'make,' 'cause,' 'create' and 'produce,' they cover almost every explanation you need.

blocks.heading: Verb + Preposition Patterns
rows: The tilt accounts for the seasons.
Victory gave rise to a new mood.
blocks.narration: These verb-plus-preposition patterns come straight from the lecture's language bank. 'Account for' means to explain: 'the tilting of the earth on its axis accounts for the change in the seasons.' 'Stem from' and 'spring from' mean to be the result of: 'Sid's determination stems from his desire to improve the world.' 'Contribute to' means to be one factor: 'mobile technology contributed to the information revolution.' 'Give rise to' means to produce: 'the country's victory gave rise to a new mood in society.' And 'derive from' means to be gained from: 'a number of benefits can be derived from this situation.'

blocks.heading: Cause-and-Effect Nouns
bullets: One explosion set off a chain reaction
effect / impact + on the audience
reason + for; precedent + for
origin / source of later problems
blocks.narration: The noun family, with their prepositions. A 'chain reaction' is a set of related events where each one causes the next: 'the incident set off a chain reaction which affected us all.' 'Effect' and 'impact' take 'on': 'the effect of the film on the audience was very powerful.' 'Reason' takes 'for' or 'why': 'the reason for his success.' 'Precedent' takes 'for': 'there are several precedents for taking such a decision' — something that already happened and gives a reason for doing it again. And 'origin' or 'source' means the beginning or cause: 'the accident was the source of her later problems.'

blocks.heading: Choose the Best Verb
blocks.problem: Choose the best verb to complete each sentence.

steps.text: Britain derived benefits from the EU.

blocks.narration: Test yourself — choose the best verb and defend the choice. 'Chocolate induces headaches in certain people' — a medical context, so 'induce.' 'Wilson's paper has generated a great deal of interest' — caused it to exist. 'The drug triggered headaches and dizziness' — sudden and negative. 'An end-of-term prize motivates students to do well' — makes them want something positive. 'The barrier inhibits the flow of water' — holds it back to prevent flooding. 'Intensive farming has contributed to the decline of bird populations' — one factor among several. And 'Britain has derived many economic benefits from membership' — gained as a result. Every choice follows the meaning column of the lecture table.

blocks.heading: Complete the Prepositions
blocks.problem: Complete each sentence with the missing word.

steps.text: no effect whatsoever on the plastic
the impact of warming on the ice caps

blocks.narration: Prepositions now, including one trap. 'De Routa's work influenced the development of computer science' — 'influence' takes a direct object, so no preposition is needed. 'The acid seemed to have no effect whatsoever on the plastic' — effect plus 'on.' 'The outcome of the meeting between the two governments' — simply 'of.' 'The reason for the failure of the project was a lack of funding' — reason plus 'for.' 'The impact of global warming on the polar ice caps' — impact plus 'on.' And 'there is no precedent for this kind of decision' — precedent plus 'for.' One sentence needed no word at all; did you spot it?

items: account FOR · stem FROM · contribute TO
effect ON · reason FOR · precedent FOR
blocks.narration: Chapter four in five lines. The gentle causes: influence, determine, motivate, facilitate. The strong causes: provoke, trigger, generate, inhibit, induce. Then the preposition pairs: account for, stem from, contribute to, give rise to, derive from. And the nouns: effect on, reason for, precedent for. Learn each verb together with its preposition, never alone. One verb, one preposition, one meaning — learn them as complete chunks.

blocks.title: Short Talks and Misleading Graphs
blocks.subtitle: How lectures are organized — and how graphs lie
blocks.narration: Chapter five. Short talks and misleading graphs. A good lecture is a guided journey: the speaker signposts every turn, and trained listeners follow easily. Learn the signposting phrases and the three-part structure — and learn how a graph can lie to you.

blocks.heading: The Three Parts of a Short Talk
bullets: Introduction — give the overview
Main points — sequenced one by one
Conclusion — pull it all together
Signposts announce what comes next
blocks.narration: Every short talk has three visible parts. The introduction gives the overview — what the lecture will cover. The main points follow, sequenced one by one. The conclusion pulls everything together. Lecturers use signposting expressions to show how the talk is organized, and recognizing them tells you what you are going to hear and in which order. Lectures also include definitions and explanations of key terms — catching those helps you take effective notes. The listening strand trains exactly this: predict the slide order, catch the main points, note the details.

blocks.heading: Signposting a Lecture
rows: In today's lecture I'd like to look at…
First, we'll look in more detail at…
Then, we'll move on to look at…
After that, we're going to see…
And then finally, I want to take…
blocks.narration: Here is the signposting skeleton of a real lecture. The overview: 'In today's lecture I'd like to look at a number of theories.' The first point: 'First, we'll look in more detail at Taylor's idea.' Next: 'Then, we'll move on to look at Maslow's hierarchy of needs.' Later: 'After that, we're going to see how Maslow influenced McGregor.' And the close: 'And then finally, I want to take a slightly different view.' When you hear these phrases, you know exactly where the lecture is going — and your notes get their structure for free.

blocks.heading: Signposts in Action: a Motivation Lecture
bullets: In today's lecture… theories of motivation
First: Taylor — money motivates everyone
Then: Maslow — five areas of needs
Finally: McClelland and Burnham — power
blocks.narration: Watch the signposts work in the motivation lecture. The speaker opens: 'In today's lecture, I'd like to look at a number of theories related to motivation at work.' First comes Taylor — money is the key motivator in the workplace. Then the lecture moves on to Maslow's famous hierarchy of needs. After that, McGregor, whose management styles were influenced by Maslow's ideas. And then finally, McClelland and Burnham, with a slightly different view. Smaller signposts help too: 'so for example' and 'an obvious example of this is' introduce examples; 'in other words' and 'how that works is' introduce explanations; 'as I said' and 'as we've already seen' refer back.

blocks.heading: How to Spot a Misleading Graph
bullets: People trust graphs more than plain claims
A zoomed or cropped axis exaggerates
A missing baseline hides the scale
Ask: what story is this graph telling?
blocks.narration: This week's TED talk asks an uncomfortable question: can a graph lie? Yes. People tend to trust graphs more than a plain claim, even though graphs can be manipulated. The vertical axis can be zoomed in or cropped, so a small difference looks dramatic. Labels, numbers, scale or context can be left out — a missing baseline hides the real proportions. The speaker's advice: look carefully at the labels, the numbers, the scale and the context, and always ask what story the graph is telling. Two ways a graph misleads: a zoomed axis, and a cropped or missing baseline.

blocks.heading: The Motivation Lecture — Check Your Notes
blocks.problem: Complete the lecture notes (Taylor, Maslow, McGregor, McClelland and Burnham).

steps.text: Maslow: five main areas of needs.

blocks.narration: Final check on your listening notes. Taylor: money motivates everyone — money is the key motivator in the workplace. Maslow: motivation equals five main areas — the hierarchy of needs has five levels, from physiological needs at the bottom to self-actualization at the top. The bottom needs are fulfilled first, and when one need is met, the next level becomes the main motivator. McGregor: management styles fall into two groups. McClelland and Burnham studied managers, and the main motivator there is power. Two more levels from the lecture: belonging — the need to feel part of a group — and security, safety and stability: job security, a stable salary, a safe working environment.

items: In today's lecture I'd like to look at…
So for example; in other words; as I said
blocks.narration: Chapter five in five lines. A short talk is introduction, main points, conclusion. The overview phrase: 'In today's lecture I'd like to look at.' The sequence: first, then, after that, finally. Examples, explanations and referring back each have their own phrases. Signposts are your note-taking skeleton. And with graphs: check the axis, the baseline, the context.

blocks.title: Noun Formation — Comparing Solutions
blocks.subtitle: Five ways to build the words you need
blocks.narration: Chapter six. Noun formation and comparing solutions. When engineers compare two solutions, they need abstract nouns: inspection, measurement, reliability. English builds them in five ways — suffixes, prefixes, roots, compound nouns and conversion — and this chapter makes you fluent in all five.

blocks.heading: Five Ways to Build Words
bullets: Suffixes: added to the end — action
Prefixes: added to the front — unhappy
Roots: inspect → inspector → inspection
Compounds: power + station
blocks.narration: Word formation has five techniques. A suffix is added to the end of a verb or an adjective to form a noun: 'act' becomes 'action.' A prefix is added to the beginning and changes the meaning, most often to a negative or a reversal: 'happy' becomes 'unhappy.' With roots, we add pieces to a root that carries the core meaning of the word family: 'inspect' gives 'inspector' and 'inspection.' Compound nouns combine two nouns into one expression, like 'power station.' And conversion — the surprise of this week — changes a word's job without changing its shape at all.

blocks.heading: Noun-Forming Suffixes
blocks.narration: Here are the six noun-forming suffixes of the lecture, with their spelling traps. '-tion' attaches to verbs: act to action, inspect to inspection, produce to production. '-ment': develop to development, measure to measurement. '-ness' attaches to adjectives: happy to happiness — watch, the y becomes an i — and dark to darkness. '-ity' also takes adjectives: able to ability, possible to possibility. '-er': build to builder, design to designer. And '-or': act to actor, generate to generator. From the cause-and-effect strand: motivate to motivation, contribute to contribution, induce to inducement.

blocks.heading: Prefixes Change the Meaning
bullets: un-: unhappy, unlock
re-: rewrite, reuse
dis-: disagree, disconnect
in-/im-: incorrect, impossible
blocks.narration: Prefixes sit at the front of a word and change its meaning — most often to a negative or a reversal. 'Un-' gives unhappy and unlock. 'Re-' means again: rewrite, reuse. 'Dis-' gives disagree and disconnect. 'In-' and 'im-' give incorrect and impossible. And 'pre-' means before: preview, preheat. The lecture's advice: for every prefix in the table, collect two more examples of your own — words you actually meet in engineering texts. Prefixes never change the part of speech: 'unhappy' is still an adjective; only the meaning flips, and that is the difference from suffixes, which build new nouns.

blocks.heading: Compound Nouns
bullets: Two nouns join into one expression
power station, solar panel, wind farm
battery pack, energy crisis
One word, two words, or a hyphen?
blocks.narration: A compound noun is a combination of two nouns written as one expression. In a typical energy article you will find 'power station,' 'solar panel,' 'wind farm,' 'battery pack,' 'energy crisis.' The lecture practises them as word networks: complete the network, guess the compound from its definition — 'she pressed it and the room lit up: the light switch' — and collect compounds from any magazine article you read. One practical warning: check in a dictionary whether the compound is written as one word, two words, or with a hyphen.

blocks.heading: Conversion — a New Job, the Same Shape
bullets: A word changes its job, not its shape
water (noun): a glass of water
water (verb): please water the plants
Teachers call it 'zero derivation'
blocks.narration: Conversion means that a word changes its job without changing its shape. No prefix, no suffix — the same word simply starts to work as a different part of speech. 'Can I have a glass of water?' — water is a noun. 'Please water the plants' — water is a verb. Compare that with the roots method, where we add pieces: 'inspect,' 'inspector,' 'inspection.' In conversion we add nothing: 'an email' becomes 'to email.' Teachers call this zero derivation, because the ending is zero. It is one reason learners can use new English words so quickly: know the noun, and you can often guess the verb.

blocks.heading: Conversion Patterns
blocks.narration: The most common conversion patterns. Noun to verb: 'I got an email' — 'email me tomorrow'; 'my phone is new' — 'I'll phone you tonight'; 'I'm reading a book' — 'we booked a table.' Verb to noun: 'I run every day' — 'I went for a run'; 'I drink tea' — 'would you like a drink?'; 'she smiled at me' — 'she has a lovely smile'; 'can you help me?' — 'thanks for your help.' Adjective to verb: 'the room is clean' — 'please clean the room'; 'the box is empty' — 'empty the box'; 'he stayed calm' — 'calm down.'

blocks.heading: How to Tell a Noun from a Verb
bullets: After a, the, my, some — a noun
After to, will, can, must — a verb
Verbs change: -s, -ed, -ing
Nouns take a/an and plurals
blocks.narration: Because the shape never changes, the sentence tells you the job of the word. Ask three questions. One: where is it? After 'a,' 'the,' 'my,' 'some' or an adjective, it is a noun — 'a drink,' 'my phone,' 'some help.' After a subject, or after 'to,' 'will,' 'can,' 'must,' it is a verb — 'I drink tea,' 'I will phone you.' Two: can it change form? Verbs take s, ed, ing — 'she emails, she emailed, she is emailing.' Nouns take 'a' or 'an' and a plural — 'an email, two emails.'

blocks.heading: The Stress Moves
bullets: a REcord — to reCORD
a PREsent — to preSENT
PROduce (food) — to proDUCE (make)
Noun stresses first; verb stresses second
blocks.narration: A small group of two-syllable words change stress instead. The noun carries stress on the first syllable, the verb on the second. 'This is my favourite record' — REcord. 'Please record the lesson' — reCORD. 'A present' — PREsent; 'to present' — preSENT. 'Fresh produce' means fruit and vegetables — PROduce; 'Japan will produce more cars' — proDUCE. A few words even change the final sound: 'a use' with a soft s, 'to use' with a z; 'a house,' 'to house.' Mark the stressed syllable in capitals when you practise: REcord, reCORD.

blocks.heading: Same Word, Different Job
blocks.problem: Write N (noun), V (verb) or Adj (adjective) for each bold word.

steps.text: Can I phone you tonight? — V
The kitchen is very clean. — Adj
I got an email from my teacher. — N

blocks.result: The sentence tells you the job
blocks.narration: Apply the three questions. 'Can I phone you tonight?' — 'phone' follows 'can,' so it is a verb. 'My phone is broken' — after 'my,' it is a noun. 'Please clean the kitchen' — an imperative, so a verb. 'The kitchen is very clean' — after 'very,' an adjective. 'Don't forget to email me the photos' — after 'to,' a verb. 'I got an email from my teacher' — after 'an,' a noun. 'We went for a long walk by the river' — 'a long walk,' a noun. 'I walk to school every day' — after 'I,' a verb. The same test catches adjectives after linking verbs: 'the kitchen is very clean.' Position decides everything.

blocks.heading: Use It as a Verb
blocks.problem: Use the word in brackets as a verb (6 items).

steps.text: I brush my hair every morning. (brush)
We have booked a table for eight.
She buttered her toast and sat down.
Please water the plants while I'm away.
Empty the box before you throw it.

blocks.narration: Now force the noun to work as a verb. 'Anna sent me a text' — 'Anna texted me this morning.' 'I use a brush for my hair' — 'I brush my hair every morning.' 'I'm reading a good book' — 'we have booked a table for eight.' 'She put butter on the toast' — 'she buttered her toast and sat down.' 'The plants need water' — 'please water the plants while I'm away.' 'The box is empty' — 'please empty the box before you throw it away.' And modern English keeps converting: 'I googled the restaurant,' 'we zoomed with our cousins,' 'he ghosted me,' 'let's bookmark this page.'

items: un-, re-, dis-, in-, pre- change meaning
blocks.narration: Chapter six in five lines. Six noun-making suffixes: tion, ment, ness, ity, er, or. Prefixes change meaning: un, re, dis, in, pre. Compounds join two nouns: power station, solar panel. Conversion changes the job, not the shape — zero derivation. And in the stress-shift pairs, the noun stresses the first syllable, the verb the second. Every technique here feeds the last skill: comparing two solutions precisely.

items: Passive = be + past participle, any tense
Graphs: rise, fall, soar, plummet, peak
increase BY 10%; increase OF 15% IN sales
Signposts: first, then, after that, finally
blocks.narration: The whole block in six lines. The passive is 'be' plus past participle, in any tense, with 'by' for the agent and 'with' for the instrument. Processes are described with the present simple passive, ordered with first, then, finally. Graphs need movement verbs — rise, fall, soar, plummet — and the preposition rule: increased by ten percent, an increase of fifteen percent in sales. Short talks run on signposts. And words are built with suffixes, prefixes, roots, compounds and conversion. That is weeks five to seven — you own it now.
